title: Alex Obadia - A Society of Agents: Trust at Machine Speed, from Bits to Atoms

segments.text: ALEX OBADIA: Hi, everyone.
I am Alex.
As mentioned, I'm part of the ARIA, Advanced Research
and Invention Agency.
Since we're a new funding agency,
I thought I would talk a little bit about what ARIA is,
and then I'll talk about the program
that we're funding, which is the main topic of this talk, which
is called Scaling Trust.
So ARIA stands for the Advanced Research and Invention Agency.
We're a UK R&D funding agency that funds R&D moonshots
worldwide.
If you're familiar with DARPA, this
would be the equivalent in the UK.
We was started only a few years ago.
And our goal is mentioned here, unlocking
scientific and technological breakthroughs that
benefit everyone.
The difference with DARPA is we don't have the D.
So we don't do anything defense-related,
but we do everything else.
Some information very quickly.
We fund public goods.
We're impact-focused.
We have a high risk appetite.
Just like DARPA, we have focus programs
that try to go after an ambitious goal.
Each of our programs is about 50 to 70 million pounds, which
is about $70 to $100 million.
And since we're three years old, we don't have a lot of programs.
But we have about 16 programs so far
in a lot of different fields, in manufacturing,
in better chips, in better vaccines or vaccines
based on different parts of the immune system,
and neurotechnologies.
And so I am a program director at ARIA.
And so I focus specifically on the program
called Scaling Trust, which is the little column you see there.
And so what is Scaling Trust?
And maybe before I do that, the goal of the talk today
is to tell you more about the things
that we're looking to fund and that we're funding already,
and also to get your opinion about the current thesis
that we have, and to let you know about this.
Great.
So Scaling Trust is currently a 50-million-pound program,
so about $70 million.
That is going to be three-year-long.
And what we care about is funding the research
and the infrastructure that enables agents to coordinate
with certain properties.
First, by coordination, we mean, can agents actually
find counterparties that they need
to maybe trade with or interact with for nontrade purposes?
Can they actually negotiate in sophisticated ways?
Can they enforce agreements as well?
And this is the thinking that we have.
Why we care about them doing this securely
is because the setting that we care about
is an adversarial setting and multiagent, multiprincipal
systems.
So we don't care about the single-owner multiagent systems.
This is about different agents that are representing different,
quote, unquote, "owners" or different principles that are
interacting securely with one another.
Why securely?
Because some of these agents may be adversarial.
They may be information asymmetry.
They might have different goals.
And so we care about what is the technology and research that
enables that.
Programmatically, because we want
this to move at machine speed, and so we don't necessarily
want humans in the loop, at scale,
we want this technology to be able to be
available to everyone.
And without intermediaries, this is
more of a statement about the topology of the future system
we want, is we want to limit the amount of systemic choke points
that exist in this infrastructure--
and the picture is blocking something.
That's OK-- across digital and physical worlds.
So we think of agents as also agents that are embodied.
So we care about building the infrastructure
that extends to the physical world as well,
and that you can have secure interactions that includes
elements of the physical world.
We think there are new developments
in cryptography and secure hardware.
In cryptography in particular, this trend
that has been dubbed programmable cryptography,
and that the latest trends in secure hardware
and in other parts of the tech stack that
enables us to break some of the tensions
that were mentioned in the previous talk as well,
or where at least the trade-off space has changed
and we can actually place different points in that space.
All right.
Why do we care about this?
One, I think, today, a lot of the agent stack
is not super mature, and it's very hard
to send our agents in a while to do stuff for us.
We've looked at a taxonomy of potential attacks before,
but there are many things there.
We're excited about a world of agent societies and agent
networks, and the value that can be created from that.
If we're able to extend this coordination infrastructure
to the physical world as well, we're
excited about potential markets that
extend to the physical world.
In a way, if we go back to the implementation of cryptography
in our modern digital society, it enabled things indirectly,
like ecommerce to exist.
And our current digital society stand on top of these building
blocks.
And so we're excited about what kind of new markets
can be created from this.
Finally, there's also specific things that agents can do that
humans cannot.
To give you an example, two agents can enter a, quote,
unquote, "room" using secure hardware.
They can potentially disclose information to one another,
and they can commit to deleting the information
from their memory if the deal doesn't go through.
And so these are things that, as humans, we
can only approximate with, for example, NDAs
that with agents we're able to do programmatically.
And so there are things that agents can uniquely
do that we're very excited by for the value that
can be created for humans and also generally these things.
However, we want to create all this value while making sure
that it's aligned with human flourishing, which
is something else that was mentioned in a previous talk.
So we want to make sure that this infrastructure is
open source.
We want to make sure that this infrastructure is open to all.
And as I mentioned, this without intermediaries point
is very important to us.
We want to enable a system where many models can exist together,
many minds can coexist together in a way.
And this concept, generally, people
talk about it in the context of pluralism or plurality.
We want to avoid a slide towards monoculture, where everyone
is using the same stack, but also, indirectly,
our preferences are also influenced in that way,
and there's less diversity in society.
It's not only about diversity for the sake of diversity,
we think.
It makes us, as humanity, less resilient to shocks,
both culturally and technologically,
and erodes our agency over time as well.
And this is really important to us.
This is why we think this should be built somehow
as a public good, and why we're very happy to give
these grants for that.
And how we do this, practically, so how
this program is structured, well, we
want to build a coordination stack for agents.
Some of this is digital.
Some of this is physical.
We're funding already a first set of teams,
including some teams at Berkeley that are, for example, working
on different ways for agents to reason about security,
to autonomously generate protocols,
and to interact with sophisticated security systems,
but also for agents to reason about negotiations
in sophisticated ways.
We're also funding-- on the physical side,
we're funding, for example, new sensors
that are more easy for agents to interact with
and that can be tamper-resistant,
and people that are trying to break these things as well.
So we have this digital-to-physical
stack that we're funding.
And a lot of this is great, but we
think, without fundamental research,
it's going to stay mostly empirical.
And a lot of the research that we see
feels very empirical to us, at least
if you come from theoretical computer science
and these fields of security.
And so we want to make sure that the stack that maybe
is arrived at or converged at an empirical matter
has a theory that underpins it.
And we think there are some new questions that
need to be answered there that is applying our formal security
thinking to this new field of AI that currently resists being
fully formalized in that sense.
And there's a few areas that we're excited about there
that I mentioned, autonomous protocol generation, formal AI
security, applying some concepts of cryptography
to the physical world as well.
If you're familiar with quantum cryptography and physically
unclonable functions.
There are a few fields there that
are trying to swap the roots of trusts
that we use in traditional cryptography
into the physical world.
And there may be others that are useful there,
and I won't go into too much detail.
So even if we have the stack, and even
if we have the theory that backs the stack
so that there's not a looming impossibility result
or we're not working completely in the dark,
we still need this to be tested, because, ultimately, this
is about multiagent, multiprinciple systems.
And we need this stack to also be stress tested.
The last thing that we're funding
is a massive test bed that is open to the public,
that anyone can submit their agents.
This stack will be tested, but you can also
bring your own stack or whatever you want.
And we're making it a competition.
So people will compete to win in this test bed.
And red teams will also be competing
to be the best red teams.
And what we want to test, essentially,
is, can we measure the state of the art
in secure agentic coordination under adversarial pressure?
Can we also see what emerges as well?
Because we can, us, as humans, decide what
the stack that is needed is.
But as we've seen many times, emergent behaviors
sometimes reveal new things that agents can uniquely do.
And so we want to make sure that the test bed
itself is open-ended enough, and the tasks themselves
are open-ended enough, that we can see what emerges from that.
And finally, and what's relevant to this track,
we want to understand what kind of failure modes exist.
A lot of these behaviors can be out of distribution.
And understanding the failure modes
help us understand the safety requirements that we need,
and maybe also regulation and these type of things.
This is kind of it.
I'm not going to go too much in the program updates,
but we are working with-- we're funding some teams already,
and we're also working with DeepMind, Cooperative AI
Foundation, and Schmidt Sciences on a call that
will close on August 8.
Some of what we're funding are the sandboxes and test
beds I mentioned here, but also other things.
And that is pretty much it.
Yeah.
Thank you very much.
I'm happy to talk more about any of this.
And if there's any skepticism or questions,
I'm happy to take them somewhere around later.
Thank you.
